quests.instruction: Say “last night” at conversation speed. What often happens to the /t/ at the end of “last”?
options: It changes into a different sound, such as [p] or [k], to match “night”
It is often left out, so “last night” sounds like “las’ night”
It stays and moves onto “night”, giving “las-tnight”
quests.correctAnswer: It is often left out, so “last night” sounds like “las’ night”
quests.hint: Say “last night” slowly, then quickly. Notice whether your tongue still touches the ridge behind your teeth between the /s/ and the /n/.
quests.explanation: In a cluster like /st/ followed by a consonant, speakers often leave out the /t/: “las’ night”. This is elision, a sound that disappears rather than one that changes into another. The /s/ and the /n/ are both still there, and the phrase means the same thing.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision is the loss of a sound in connected speech; a word-final /t/ after /s/ is frequently omitted before a following consonant.

quests.instruction: Compare “last night” with “train pass”. In which phrase does a sound change into a different sound rather than disappear?
options: “train pass”: the /n/ becomes [m] before the /p/
“last night”: the /t/ becomes [n] to match the /n/
Both phrases: every connected-speech change replaces one sound with another
quests.correctAnswer: “train pass”: the /n/ becomes [m] before the /p/
quests.hint: In one phrase a consonant is simply absent; in the other it is still there but made in a different place.
quests.explanation: In “last night” the /t/ is missing: that is elision. In “train pass” the /n/ is still present but moves to the lips ([m]) because of the /p/: that is assimilation. So disappearing and changing are different things, and they give the listener different clues.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision removes a segment, whereas assimilation replaces it with a similar segment; the difference can be tested by asking whether the sound is absent or merely produced differently.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “fast food” best: a sound disappearing, changing, or simply staying?
options: Staying: the /t/ is fully released and moves onto “food” as a separate sound
Changing: the /t/ becomes an /f/ to match the next sound in the phrase
Disappearing: the /t/ is often left out before the /f/ of “food”
quests.correctAnswer: Disappearing: the /t/ is often left out before the /f/ of “food”
quests.hint: Say the phrase quickly and notice whether you can feel the tongue tip touch the ridge for a /t/ before the /f/ starts.
quests.explanation: The final /t/ of “fast” sits between /s/ and /f/, a crowded spot, so it is often omitted: “fas’ food”. Because the /t/ is simply missing, this is elision. The three-way test (gone, different, or still there) tells you which pattern you are hearing.
quests.phoneticRule: A useful diagnostic is the three-way test: if the sound is absent it is elision, if it is present but altered it is assimilation or a variant, and if it is present and moved it is linking.

quests.instruction: Say “best friend” as you would when introducing someone. What happens to the final /t/ of “best”?
options: It is often left out, giving “bes’ friend”
It becomes an /f/ to match the /f/ of “friend”
It stays fully released and is followed by a short pause
quests.correctAnswer: It is often left out, giving “bes’ friend”
quests.hint: Compare “best” on its own with “best friend” at normal speed. Which version lets your tongue skip a step?
quests.explanation: “Best” ends in /st/, and “friend” begins with a consonant, so the /t/ sits between two other consonant sounds. That is a very common place for speakers to leave it out: “bes’ friend”. The word is still “best”; the /t/ is simply not pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /t/ after /s/ is commonly omitted when the next word begins with a consonant, reducing a three-consonant sequence.

quests.instruction: Why does “most people” often sound like “mos’ people”?
options: The /t/ sits between /s/ and /p/, so it is easily dropped in quick speech
The word “most” is simply replaced by the different word “mos” in casual speech
The /s/ moves onto “people”, so the phrase is heard as “mo-speople”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ sits between /s/ and /p/, so it is easily dropped in quick speech
quests.hint: Count the consonants in a row at the boundary: /s/, /t/, then /p/. Which one is easiest to leave out?
quests.explanation: A run of three consonants (/s/, /t/, /p/) is awkward to say quickly, so the middle one, /t/, often drops out. The result is “mos’ people”. The speaker has not changed the word; the sound has gone because the cluster was simplified.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant clusters across word boundaries are simplified by omitting the middle stop, especially /t/ and /d/ between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “just now” in “Someone saw him just now.” Which version shows elision?
options: “just now”, with a clear /t/ released before the /n/
“jus-tnow”, with the /t/ moved onto “now”
“jus’ now”, with the /t/ left out
quests.correctAnswer: “jus’ now”, with the /t/ left out
quests.hint: The /t/ sits between /s/ and /n/. Predict what is likely to happen, then look at the options.
quests.explanation: The /t/ in “just” is in the same position as in “best friend”: after /s/ and before a consonant. So it is often omitted: “jus’ now”. Notice that /n/ is not a lip or back sound, so this is not a place change; it is a plain loss of the /t/.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision of /t/ after /s/ does not depend on the following consonant's place; it applies before nasals, stops and fricatives alike.

quests.instruction: You describe a neighbour: “He’s a nice old man.” Which spoken form of “old man” fits elision?
options: “old man”, with a fully released /d/ before the /m/
“ob man”, with the /d/ changing into a /b/ before the /m/
“ol’ man”, with the /d/ left out after the /l/
quests.correctAnswer: “ol’ man”, with the /d/ left out after the /l/
quests.hint: Say “old” on its own, then “old man” at conversation speed. Notice whether your tongue taps the ridge a second time after the /l/.
quests.explanation: The /d/ at the end of “old” follows /l/ and comes before /m/, so it is a prime candidate for omission: “ol’ man”. The /l/ and the vowel stay, and the meaning is unchanged. The same happens in many phrases where /ld/ or /nd/ meets a consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /d/ in /ld/ and /nd/ clusters is often omitted when a consonant follows, especially in frequent phrases.

quests.instruction: In “kind words”, which sound is most likely to disappear in fast speech?
options: The /n/ in the middle of “kind”
The /d/ at the very end of “kind”
The /w/ at the start of “words”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ at the very end of “kind”
quests.hint: Only a sound at the edge of a cluster is at risk. Which sound is last in the cluster before the next word begins?
quests.explanation: In /nd/ the /n/ is a nasal and the /d/ is a stop made at the same place. The /d/ is the weaker, more predictable member, so it is the one that tends to go: “kine’ words”. The /n/ stays, because it carries the nasal sound of the word.
quests.phoneticRule: In nasal + stop clusters (/nd/, /ld/, /nt/) the stop is the member most often omitted before a consonant.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “grand final”. Which version shows elision?
options: “grand final”, with the /d/ released clearly before the /f/
“gran’ final”, with the /d/ left out after the /n/
“grand-final”, with the /d/ moving onto the start of “final”
quests.correctAnswer: “gran’ final”, with the /d/ left out after the /n/
quests.hint: Say “grand final” quickly, as a commentator would. Listen for whether the /d/ is still there.
quests.explanation: “Grand” ends in /nd/, and “final” begins with a consonant, so the /d/ is often omitted: “gran’ final”. The nasal stays, so the word is still recognisable. Sports commentary is a good place to hear this reduction.
quests.phoneticRule: The omission of /d/ in /nd/ clusters before a consonant is regular across word classes, including adjectives such as “grand” and nouns such as “friend”.

quests.instruction: Predict what happens to the /t/ in “perfect day” in fast speech.
options: It stays fully released before the /d/ of “day”
It moves onto “day” and is released as “perfec-tday”
It is often left out, leaving “perfec’ day”
quests.correctAnswer: It is often left out, leaving “perfec’ day”
quests.hint: Look at the sounds in a row at the end of “perfect”: /k/ and /t/. Then think about what follows.
quests.explanation: “Perfect” ends in /kt/, and “day” starts with a consonant, so the final /t/ is often omitted: “perfec’ day”. The /k/ remains, which keeps the word recognisable. Clusters ending in /kt/ appear in many common words.
quests.phoneticRule: Stop + /t/ clusters (/kt/, /pt/) frequently lose the final /t/ before a following consonant.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “kept quiet” sounding like “kep’ quiet”.
options: The /p/ disappears, because it is a weaker and quieter sound than the /t/ that follows it
The final /t/ is omitted because it sits between /p/ and the /kw/ of “quiet”
The /t/ moves onto the start of “quiet”, giving “kep-tquiet”
quests.correctAnswer: The final /t/ is omitted because it sits between /p/ and the /kw/ of “quiet”
quests.hint: Ask which sound of the cluster /pt/ sits right next to the next word.
quests.explanation: “Kept” ends in /pt/, and “quiet” starts with /kw/. The /t/ is wedged between /p/ and /k/, and a closure of the tongue tip there is barely audible, so it is often left out: “kep’ quiet”. The /p/ stays because the word needs it to be recognisable.
quests.phoneticRule: In a cluster of stops, the middle or last stop that is followed by another stop is the one most likely to be omitted.

quests.instruction: In an advert you hear “Act now!” Which version of “act now” shows elision?
options: “ac’ now”, with the /t/ left out
“act now”, with a clear /t/ and a pause
“ac-tnow”, with the /t/ moving onto “now”
quests.correctAnswer: “ac’ now”, with the /t/ left out
quests.hint: The word ends in /kt/ and the next word begins with /n/. Predict the /t/ first.
quests.explanation: “Act” ends in /kt/, and “now” begins with a consonant, so the /t/ often disappears: “ac’ now”. Adverts and notices are often said quickly, so this reduced form is common even in clear speech.
quests.phoneticRule: The omission pattern is the same for /kt/ in short words as for longer words: the final /t/ drops before a consonant.

quests.instruction: Compare “last night” and “last evening”. Why is the /t/ much more likely to disappear in “last night”?
options: “Night” is a longer word than “evening”, so the /t/ gets lost behind it
Before a consonant the /t/ is crowded, while before a vowel it links onto the next word
The vowel in “evening” strengthens the /t/ by voicing it, so it cannot be lost
“Last night” is a fixed expression, so every sound in it is optional in speech and can be removed
quests.correctAnswer: Before a consonant the /t/ is crowded, while before a vowel it links onto the next word
quests.hint: Think about what follows the /t/ in each phrase: a consonant or a vowel.
quests.explanation: Before a vowel, the /t/ can move onto the next syllable, so “last evening” is heard as “las-tevening”. Before a consonant there is no vowel to carry it, and the /st/ cluster plus another consonant is crowded, so the /t/ is often omitted. So elision is much more likely before consonants than before vowels.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision of word-final /t/ and /d/ is typical before a consonant; before a vowel the same sounds are normally retained and linked.

quests.instruction: In “most of them” the /t/ usually stays. Why?
quests.word: Staff watched most of them leave
quests.textToSpeak: Staff watched most of them leave
options: “Of” is too weak a word to take any consonant from the word before it
The speaker is being careful, which cancels connected speech in that phrase
The /t/ is replaced by a /k/ before “of”, because /k/ is easier to say
A vowel follows, so the /t/ can link onto “of” instead of being omitted entirely
quests.correctAnswer: A vowel follows, so the /t/ can link onto “of” instead of being omitted entirely
quests.hint: Compare the sound that follows the /t/ in “most of them” with the sound that follows it in “most people”.
quests.explanation: In “most of them”, the vowel of “of” follows the /t/, so the /t/ links onto it: “mo-sta them”. In “most people” there is a consonant after the /t/, so omission is likely. The same word can therefore keep or lose its /t/ depending on what follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Whether a word-final /t/ is retained depends on the following sound: before vowels it links, before consonants it may be omitted.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “first offer” keeps its /t/ because a vowel follows?
options: “fur-stoffer”, with the /t/ linking onto the word “offer”
“fur’ offer”, with the /t/ omitted
“fur-soffer”, with the /s/ moved but the /t/ lost
“first … offer”, with a clear stop and a long pause
quests.correctAnswer: “fur-stoffer”, with the /t/ linking onto the word “offer”
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of “offer”. What does it allow the /t/ to do?
quests.explanation: “Offer” begins with a vowel, so the /t/ of “first” is carried onto it: “fur-stoffer”. This is the linking you learned in Stage 2. Elision needs a following consonant, so it does not apply here.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking and elision are complementary: the same word-final consonant links before a vowel and may be omitted before a consonant.

quests.instruction: In many varieties of English the /t/ in “wet day” is not released clearly. What is often happening to it?
options: It is deleted completely, leaving no trace of a closure at all between the two words
It changes into a /d/ to match the /d/ of “day”, so both are voiced alike
It is often unreleased or made as a throat stop, so it is quieter but not absent
It moves onto the start of “day” and is released there with a puff of air
quests.correctAnswer: It is often unreleased or made as a throat stop, so it is quieter but not absent
quests.hint: Say “wet day” and notice whether your throat or tongue still makes a closure before the /d/, even if you do not hear a clear /t/.
quests.explanation: At the end of a word before a consonant, /t/ is often not released with a puff of air; in many accents it is produced as a quick throat closure instead. That makes it less prominent, but it is still a closure, which is why it differs from a true elision, where nothing is left. Listeners often use the quick closure to tell “wet day” from a phrase with no /t/ at all.
quests.phoneticRule: Final /t/ before a consonant is frequently unreleased or glottalised; this reduces its prominence without removing the closure, so it is not elision.

quests.instruction: Compare “wet day”, “short break” and “left side”. In which one is the /t/ most likely to be truly absent?
options: “wet day”: the /t/ is absent because it is not released
“short break”: the /t/ is absent because it has become a /p/
“left side”: the /t/ sits between /f/ and /s/ and is often omitted
None of them: a /t/ that cannot be heard is still being produced as a closure
quests.correctAnswer: “left side”: the /t/ sits between /f/ and /s/ and is often omitted
quests.hint: A /t/ that is only softened is still a closure; a /t/ that is truly absent leaves nothing between its neighbours.
quests.explanation: In “wet day” the /t/ is softened to a throat stop or an unreleased closure, and in “short break” it moves to the lips: neither is elision. In “left side” the /t/ sits between /f/ and /s/, a crowded cluster, and is often left out entirely: “lef’ side”. Telling these three apart prevents you from labelling every quiet /t/ as elision.
quests.phoneticRule: Three outcomes must be distinguished: elision (absent), assimilation (altered place) and unreleased or glottal realisation (present but less audible).

quests.instruction: A speaker says “right now” with a short throat stop where the /t/ was. Which description is best?
options: Elision: the /t/ has gone completely, leaving no closure at all
Assimilation: the /t/ has taken the place of the /n/ that follows it
Linking: the /t/ moves onto the start of “now”
A glottal or unreleased /t/: reduced, but not truly absent
quests.correctAnswer: A glottal or unreleased /t/: reduced, but not truly absent
quests.hint: Notice whether there is still a brief closure in the throat or mouth where the /t/ should be.
quests.explanation: A short throat stop in place of /t/ is a common casual realisation in many varieties of British English. Because a closure is still produced, the /t/ is reduced rather than deleted. Classifying it correctly helps you listen for the closure instead of expecting a missing sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Glottal reinforcement or replacement is a reduction of /t/, not its deletion, and it is more typical of some accents than others.

quests.instruction: Say “probably” quickly, as in “Everything is probably fine.” How many syllables do you often hear?
options: Often just two: “prob’ly”, with the middle syllable left out
Four: every vowel is pronounced, even in casual speech
Three: the last syllable is dropped, giving “pro-ba”
Five: speakers add an extra vowel to separate the consonants
quests.correctAnswer: Often just two: “prob’ly”, with the middle syllable left out
quests.hint: Say “probably” at conversation speed and tap one finger for each syllable you actually produce.
quests.explanation: In casual speech “probably” is often said as “prob’ly”: the unstressed middle syllable loses its vowel and is left out. This is elision inside a word, and it makes the word shorter without changing the stressed syllable. Many dictionaries note the shorter form as a normal variant.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed syllables in common words, especially those with a weak vowel between consonants, are often reduced or omitted in casual speech.

quests.instruction: Which sound is usually missing in “camera” as people say it quickly, as in “a digital camera”?
options: The /m/ in the middle, so it sounds like “ca-ra”
The weak vowel in the middle, so it sounds like “cam’ra” in a quick, casual style
The final weak vowel at the end, so it sounds like “camer”
The first /k/ at the start, so it sounds like “amera”
quests.correctAnswer: The weak vowel in the middle, so it sounds like “cam’ra” in a quick, casual style
quests.hint: Say “camera” at normal speed and notice how many distinct vowels you actually produce.
quests.explanation: “Camera” has three written syllables, but the weak vowel between /m/ and /r/ is often lost, giving “cam’ra”. The stressed first syllable and the final weak vowel remain. Hearing the shorter form prevents you from expecting an extra syllable.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak vowel between two consonants in an unstressed syllable is a frequent site of elision, especially before /r/ and /l/.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “interesting” in “Today was really interesting.” Which spoken form is typical?
options: “in-ter-es-ting”: four syllables, all vowels pronounced
“in-ter-esting”: three syllables, with the /t/ dropped instead of the vowel
“in-res-ting”: three syllables, with the /t/ and the vowel both dropped
“in-tresting”: three syllables, with the weak vowel after the /t/ gone
quests.correctAnswer: “in-tresting”: three syllables, with the weak vowel after the /t/ gone
quests.hint: Compare how many syllables you write with how many a fast speaker produces.
quests.explanation: “Interesting” is written with four syllables, but speakers often drop the weak vowel after the /t/: “in-tresting”. The /t/ stays, which keeps the word recognisable. Reduced forms like this are normal in everyday speech and in broadcasts.
quests.phoneticRule: Words with stressed first syllables and several weak syllables often lose a weak vowel, so the syllable count in speech is lower than in the spelling.

quests.instruction: In “next month”, the /t/ often goes missing. Is that elision or assimilation?
options: Assimilation: the /t/ becomes an /m/ to match the first sound of “month”
Elision: the /t/ is simply left out, with no other sound taking its place at all
Linking: the /t/ moves onto the start of “month” and is released there
Assimilation: the /t/ becomes a /p/ made at the lips
quests.correctAnswer: Elision: the /t/ is simply left out, with no other sound taking its place at all
quests.hint: Ask whether a different sound has appeared in place of the /t/ or whether there is simply a gap.
quests.explanation: In “next month” the /t/ is gone, but nothing replaces it: you hear “nex’ month”. That is elision. In assimilation, the sound would still be present in a changed form, such as [p] before /m/. The test is whether a substitute sound appears.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision and assimilation can affect the same sound, and the difference lies in whether the segment is absent or replaced by a different segment.

quests.instruction: In “handbag”, two things often happen in casual speech. Which pair is right?
options: The /d/ is omitted (elision), and the /n/ shifts to /m/ (assimilation)
The /d/ becomes /b/ (assimilation), and the /n/ is omitted (elision)
Both the /d/ and the /n/ are omitted, so only “ha” and “bag” remain (elision)
Only the /n/ shifts to /m/, and the /d/ is released before the /b/
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ is omitted (elision), and the /n/ shifts to /m/ (assimilation)
quests.hint: Separate the two sounds of the cluster /nd/ and ask what happens to each one before the /b/.
quests.explanation: The /d/ is the weaker member of /nd/, so it is often left out: that is elision. The remaining /n/ then meets /b/, a lip sound, and shifts to [m]: that is assimilation. One short word can therefore show two processes in sequence: “ham bag”.
quests.phoneticRule: Processes can feed each other: omission of a cluster member can leave a nasal adjacent to a bilabial, which then assimilates in place.

quests.instruction: In “round table”, the /d/ before the /t/ is often missing. Which description fits?
quests.word: Join us at the round table
quests.textToSpeak: Join us at the round table
options: Assimilation: the /d/ shifts to the back of the mouth to match the following /t/
Assimilation: the /n/ shifts to the lips before /t/
Elision of the /d/ only: the /n/ stays alveolar because /t/ is also alveolar
Elision of the /n/: the nasal vanishes and the /d/ stays
quests.correctAnswer: Elision of the /d/ only: the /n/ stays alveolar because /t/ is also alveolar
quests.hint: Check where /n/, /d/ and /t/ are each made. If they share a place, what kind of change is left?
quests.explanation: /n/, /d/ and /t/ are all alveolar, so there is no place mismatch for assimilation to resolve. The only change likely here is omission of the /d/: “roun’ table”. Remember that assimilation needs a different place; elision needs only a crowded cluster.
quests.phoneticRule: When neighbouring consonants share a place of articulation, assimilation of place has nothing to change, leaving elision as the likely reduction.
quests.spokenForm: Join us at the roun’ table

quests.instruction: Which two sounds are often omitted in the quick sentence “Oops, I just missed the bus”?
quests.word: Oops, I just missed the bus
quests.textToSpeak: Oops, I just missed the bus
options: The /s/ of “just” and the /s/ of “missed”
The /j/ of “just” and the /m/ of “missed”
The /t/ of “just” and the /ð/ of “the”
The /t/ of “just” and the /t/ of “missed”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “just” and the /t/ of “missed”
quests.hint: Look for two word-final /t/ sounds that are each followed by a consonant.
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/ before “missed”, which begins with /m/, so its /t/ is often omitted. “Missed” ends in /st/ before “the”, so its /t/ can also go. The sentence is then heard as “Oops, I jus’ mis’ the bus”. Notice that the other sounds are all present, so the sentence remains understandable.
quests.phoneticRule: In a sentence, each word-final /st/ before a consonant is a separate site where /t/ may be omitted.
quests.spokenForm: Oops, I jus’ mis’ the bus

quests.instruction: In “Sorry, we lost track of time”, one boundary shows elision and another shows linking. Which pair is right?
quests.word: Sorry, we lost track of time
quests.textToSpeak: Sorry, we lost track of time
options: Linking at “lost track”, elision at “track of”
Elision at “lost track”, and elision at “track of”
Elision at “lost track”, linking at “track of”, in the same sentence
Linking at both boundaries
quests.correctAnswer: Elision at “lost track”, linking at “track of”, in the same sentence
quests.hint: At one boundary a consonant has a consonant after it; at the other, it has a vowel after it. What does each situation allow?
quests.explanation: At “lost track”, the /t/ of “lost” is followed by a consonant, so it is often omitted: “los’ track”. At “track of”, the /k/ is followed by a vowel, so it links onto “of”: “tra-kuv”. Same sentence, two different outcomes, decided by what follows each consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant is a candidate for elision before a consonant and for linking before a vowel; the following sound selects which process applies.

quests.instruction: A friend suggests something unlikely and you reply, “You must be joking.” Which spoken form of “must be” shows elision?
options: “mus’ be”, with the /t/ omitted before the /b/ of “be” entirely
“must be”, with a clear /t/ released before the /b/
“mub be”, with the /t/ changing into a /b/
“mus-tbe”, with the /t/ moving onto “be”
quests.correctAnswer: “mus’ be”, with the /t/ omitted before the /b/ of “be” entirely
quests.hint: The /t/ sits between /s/ and /b/. Decide whether it is gone, changed, or moved.
quests.explanation: “Must” ends in /st/, and “be” begins with a consonant, so the /t/ is often left out: “mus’ be”. Because nothing replaces it, this is elision rather than assimilation. The phrase is common in conversation, so the reduced form is very familiar to listeners.
quests.phoneticRule: Modal verbs ending in /st/, such as “must”, regularly lose the /t/ before a consonant in casual speech.

quests.instruction: In a fast “short break”, the /t/ often sounds like a /p/. Is the /t/ missing, changed or just softer?
options: Missing: the /t/ has been omitted entirely
Changed: the /t/ has become a /p/ made at the lips
Just softer: the /t/ is unreleased but still made with the tongue tip
Unchanged: it is the same /t/ with a short pause after it
quests.correctAnswer: Changed: the /t/ has become a /p/ made at the lips
quests.hint: Ask where the closure is made now, and whether it is the same place as before.
quests.explanation: In “short break” the closure is no longer made with the tongue tip but with the lips, and a /p/-like sound is heard. That is a changed sound, so it is assimilation, not elision. If the /t/ were missing there would be no closure at all, and if it were softer it would still be made at the same place.
quests.phoneticRule: A sound that appears in a new place of articulation is assimilated; a sound with no closure is elided; a sound with a weaker closure at the same place is merely reduced.

quests.instruction: A speaker says “boat trip” with a quick throat stop where the /t/ would be. Is the /t/ missing, changed or just softer?
options: Missing: nothing at all is left between “boa” and “trip”, so the /t/ has been omitted
Changed: the /t/ has become a /k/ made at the back of the mouth
Linking: the /t/ has moved onto the start of “trip” as a separate sound
Just softer: a closure is still made, so the /t/ is reduced, not removed
quests.correctAnswer: Just softer: a closure is still made, so the /t/ is reduced, not removed
quests.hint: Listen for whether a brief closure remains where the /t/ should be.
quests.explanation: A throat stop keeps a closure, so the /t/ is reduced rather than removed. In elision the closure would disappear altogether, and in assimilation it would be made at a different place. Here the same slot is occupied by a weaker version of the same sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Reduction without loss (glottalisation or lack of release) must be separated from elision by checking for a remaining closure.

quests.instruction: In a quick “post box”, you hear “pos’ box”. Which label fits the /t/?
options: Changed: the /t/ has become a /b/ made at the lips
Just softer: the /t/ is only unreleased, with a closure still made between the /s/ and the /b/
Missing: the /t/ has been omitted between /s/ and /b/
Linking: the /t/ moves onto the start of “box”
quests.correctAnswer: Missing: the /t/ has been omitted between /s/ and /b/
quests.hint: Check whether any closure remains between the /s/ and the /b/, and whether any other sound has appeared.
quests.explanation: Between /s/ and /b/ the /t/ is crowded and often disappears completely: “pos’ box”. No closure remains and no other sound replaces it, so this is true elision. Compare this with “short break” and “boat trip”, where something is still produced in the /t/ slot.
quests.phoneticRule: True elision leaves no trace: there is no closure and no substitute sound, which separates it from assimilation and from reduced variants.
